transcript:
[00:00] Priya (Redwood): Hi Marta, thanks for making time — can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Marta (Phoenix): Yes, loud and clear. Thanks Priya. We kicked this to get more concrete about dedicated on-prem options and how bursting would work, so happy to walk through our constraints.
[00:15] Priya: Great. Quick intros — I'm Priya, AE, and Ethan's our SE who will map out the ops details.
[00:22] Ethan (Redwood SE): Hey team. Quick note: we'll cover topology, isolation, prewarm, and failover paths.
[00:28] Daniel (Phoenix, Infra): Quick context — we run a multi-tenant inference layer for our app, currently self-hosting smaller models but need capacity for launch in Q3. Primary ask: reserved GPUs on-prem for performance and data residency.
[00:40] Marta: Also isolation. We frequently run different customers' workloads and need hard tenant separation for some regulated customers.
[00:47] Aisha (Security): From security side we need KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, and a SOC2-equivalent paper trail. On-prem is preferred because of compliance reviewers.
[00:56] Priya: Understood. To confirm, you're evaluating three modes in parallel — hosted for dev/scale, Dedicated reserved for production, and Private on-prem for regulated tenants?
[01:05] Marta: That's right. We like Redwood's ability to provide the same API across those modes — keeps our code simpler.
[01:12] Ethan: Good. For dedicated on-prem, we typically install the customer control plane and the serving runtime lives in your cluster. You can pin model versions and we provide operators + docs. For burst we offer warm-pool strategies or fallback to Redwood-hosted endpoints if you allow network egress.
[01:28] Daniel: That fallback is a hard point. Legal may not let traffic go off-prem for certain customers. For others, it's ok. We need a mixed policy.
[01:36] Priya: Makes sense — hybrid fallback by workload class is doable. We'll capture that in the runbook.
[01:42] Marta: Can you explain the warm pool approach vs prewarming reserved nodes? We got different answers internally.
[01:49] Ethan: Sure. Two patterns: 1) Hot/warm pool where instances stay preloaded with model KV cache so cold start time is minimal — this costs running GPUs idle but gives low p99 latency. 2) On-demand prewarm which spins GPUs when burst triggers; cheaper but higher spike latency. We can also combine with smaller local quantized variants for instantaneous fallbacks.
[02:10] Daniel: How do you handle tenant fencing? If we have a node failure during burst, does one tenant affect others?
[02:18] Ethan: We have isolation topologies — node-per-tenant, strict GPU partitioning, or soft multi-tenancy with cgroup limits. On-prem customers often choose node-per-tenant for regulated workloads; it's the safest for blast radius.
[02:31] Aisha: Node-per-tenant sounds expensive, can you share rough numbers?
[02:35] Ethan: We'll run footprint modeling — depends on model size and concurrency. For example, 8xA100-style equivalents for high-concurrency LLMs vs 1-2 GPUs for small rerankers. We'll include concurrency profiles in the spreadsheet.
[02:50] Marta: What about preemption from cloud/hypervisor? We run VMware and K8s — what do you support?
[02:56] Ethan: We mostly integrate with Kubernetes. On-prem we support standard K8s distributions; we can also provide a hardened operator for node scheduling and GPU allocation. Preemption policies are configurable; reserved nodes are pinned to avoid eviction.
[03:10] Daniel: And encryption? We must use our KMS and HSM for key management.
[03:14] Priya: We support customer-managed keys (KMS) and can integrate with common HSM providers. We'll share the integration checklist.
[03:21] Aisha: How are audit logs surfaced? We need immutable logs for individual API calls for compliance.
[03:25] Ethan: The platform can emit detailed per-request traces and audit events to your collector — we support syslog, S3-compatible sinks, and direct SIEM integrations. Retention policies are configurable on your side.
[03:36] Marta: Latency expectations — our product SLO is 150ms p95 for single-turn chat. Can Redwood meet that on-prem?
[03:44] Ethan: Yes, with dedicated GPUs and warm pools we commonly hit sub-100ms p95 for optimized models. But quantization, sequence length, and model family matter. We'll profile with your typical prompt distribution.
[03:57] Daniel: About burst day — we have marketing spikes where concurrency quadruples for a few hours. Is autoscaling fast enough?
[04:04] Ethan: We support autoscaling policies that combine local warm pools, prewarmed spare nodes, and optional overflow to hosted Redwood if allowed. Autoscale is tuned to your pod startup times; we'd recommend a small hot pool sized for expected spikes plus a standby reserve.
[04:18] Priya: On pricing: reserved capacity has a monthly commit; bursts on top can be priced as on-demand or via scheduled capacity. We'll send a model sheet.
[04:26] Marta: We need to understand cost delta between node-per-tenant and shared-pool with QoS.
[04:31] Priya: We'll include scenario examples in the spreadsheet.
[04:36] Daniel: Any limits on model types? We run some with large KV caches (long context).
[04:40] Ethan: Long-context models are supported; memory and KV cache management matter. The runtime supports KV sharding and continuous batching to reduce cost. We'll analyze memory footprint per context length.
[04:52] Marta: How do you validate that fallback to hosted keeps privacy and does not leak data?
[04:58] Priya: We treat fallback as policy-driven. For regulated tenants you can mark requests as non-eligible for offsite processing; for others we encrypt in transit and can route through a dedicated tenant in the hosted environment. We can show the flow and encryption details in the security doc.
[05:15] Aisha: We will also require that logs of regulated tenants never leave our environment; is that supported?
[05:20] Ethan: Yes — you can disable log export for certain namespaces and keep audit trails local.
[05:26] Marta: What's typical lead time for on-prem install and validation?
[05:30] Priya: Usually 4–8 weeks depending on access, network approvals, and POC scope. If it's a straightforward k8s install with our operator it's closer to 4 weeks.
[05:38] Daniel: We expect to run a 2-week benchmark POC that simulates burst windows. Can Redwood help with load generation?
[05:44] Ethan: Absolutely. We can provide scripts and help set up controlled injections. We'll also run side-by-side hosted vs local to show delta.
[05:51] Marta: For timelines — our procurement window is end of April, want production by July. Is that reasonable?
[05:56] Priya: Yes, that aligns with a March POC, April procurement, May install, and June validation. July production is doable.
[06:04] Daniel: One more — how do we handle model updates and rollbacks in on-prem?
[06:09] Ethan: We support pinned model versions, canaries, and quick rollbacks. The operator provides versioned manifests and an A/B style rollout.
[06:18] Marta: Any gotchas we should know?
[06:20] Ethan: Watch sequence length and KV cache sizing — costs jump quickly with long contexts. Also warm pools increase baseline cost. And ensure network egress policies are approved if you want hosted fallback.
[06:32] Priya: Ok, quick recap of next steps: Ethan will produce the footprint/cost models, I'll send pricing and contract template, and we'll share security/KMS docs. Phoenix will share traffic patterns and compliance list.
[06:45] Marta: Sounds good. We'll loop in procurement and legal after we see the pricing.
[06:50] Aisha: We'll also review the SOC2 docs and send any additional requirements.
[06:54] Priya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the POC kickoff invite.
[06:58] Daniel: Thanks all, appreciate it.
[07:00] Priya: End call.

Notes: Transcript auto-generated; minor mis-hearings possible (e.g., K V cache transcribed as spelled letters). Links referenced during call: Dedicated pricing spreadsheet (link shared by Priya post-call), SOC2 + KMS integration doc (Redwood internal share).
